title: Gorge Walking in Snowdonia
strapline: Leap, scramble, and swim your way through Snowdonia's breathtaking canyons — the ultimate wet adventure.
metaTitle: Gorge Walking Snowdonia | The Complete Guide | Adventure Wales
metaDescription: Discover the best gorge walking Snowdonia has to offer. Routes, operators, gear, and everything you need for an unforgettable canyoning experience.
heroAlt: Gorge walker leaps into a pool of water in a Snowdonia canyon.
introduction:
First, a scope note — because the words gorge walking and canyoning get used interchangeably in Snowdonia, and they shouldn't be. Gorge walking, on this page, means a guided wet scramble up a river gorge — wading, scrambling, the occasional short jump into a plunge pool. Feet stay close to the rock; ropes aren't usually load-bearing. Canyoning is the rope-led discipline that descends the same terrain — abseils down waterfalls, controlled jumps, swims through tighter slots. The Snowdonia operators below offer both, often using the same valleys, but the experience and the skill bar are different. Where we know an operator runs canyoning-grade trips into a given gorge, we've flagged it.

That caveat aside, Snowdonia is genuinely one of the best gorge-walking destinations in the UK, for one geological reason: the glacier-scoured Ogwen, Llugwy and Glaslyn valleys cut through hard volcanic rock that holds its shape — clean granite-style slabs, sculpted plunge pools, and reliable bedrock to scramble on. You're not slipping over greasy mudstone. The water is cold even in August (8–12°C in the higher pools), but the gorges drain steeply, so a good summer week firms conditions up fast.

The scene splits across roughly four valleys. The Ogwen Valley (lower and upper sections below Llyn Idwal) is the classic guided introduction — Ogwen Cottage is the standard meeting point, and Mountainxperience and Plas y Brenin all run regular trips here. Ceunant Mawr at Llanberis — the dramatic waterfall canyon directly above the village (Welsh for 'great ravine') — is the local canyoning grade-up: short approach, big features, mostly run as a canyoning descent rather than an upward gorge walk, and the natural step up from the Ogwen day. The Nant Gwynant valley below the Watkin Path holds longer, more remote routes for experienced walkers. Fairy Glen at Betws-y-Coed, Conwy Falls and the Aberglaslyn Pass near Beddgelert are the family/sightseeing end — paddle-and-scramble in shallow pools rather than full gorge days.

The weather rule on every Snowdonia gorge: water level beats every other variable. A dry forecast on the day means nothing if the previous 48 hours dumped rain on the catchment above — Ogwen, Llugwy and Glaslyn all spike fast and drain slow. Operators read this for you. If you're going self-guided, check Natural Resources Wales river levels (Llanrwst gauge on the Conwy, Betws-y-Coed on the Llugwy) before you set off, and pick another day if the trace is sitting high. The Dolgarrog gorge listed below is included as a documented expert route — it has killed people, and it's not a self-guided option for anyone without serious canyoning experience and a strong team.

spots.name: Ogwen Valley Gorge (Lower)
spots.description: A classic introduction to gorge walking. This section of the Ogwen Valley gorge offers a good mix of wading, easy scrambles, and small jumps into clear pools. It's a popular spot, so expect some company, especially during peak season. Expect stunning views of Tryfan looming overhead.
spots.bestFor: Beginners and families with older children
spots.notSuitableFor: Very young children or those with limited mobility.
spots.parking: Limited parking at the Ogwen Cottage car park (charges apply). Arrive early, especially on weekends.
spots.insiderTip: Avoid peak times by going early in the morning or later in the afternoon. The light is often better then, too.
spots.howToDoIt: Most people do this as a guided half-day: meet at Ogwen Cottage, kit up in wetsuit, buoyancy aid and helmet, then work upstream from the road, wading through pools and scrambling low rock steps with a handful of small jumps (a metre or two) into deep pools along the way. Guides scale the route to the group, so nervous first-timers can climb down rather than jump. No prior gorge or scrambling experience is needed for this section.
spots.access: Start from the Ogwen Cottage / Ogwen Centre car park on the A5 — it's a short walk down to the river from there. The car park is pay-and-display, cashless, and fills early on weekends, so arrive before mid-morning in summer.
spots.routeDescription: Working upstream from the road bridge, the lower Ogwen gorge alternates wide, wadeable pools with short scrambled rock steps, framed by Tryfan's east face rising directly above. It's a forgiving line — nothing forces a jump, and escape onto the bank is possible at most points — which is why it's the standard guided introduction for this whole region.

spots.name: Swallow Falls Gorge (View from above, not in the river)
spots.description: While you can't actually gorge walk in Swallow Falls (it's far too dangerous), the surrounding area offers stunning views of the cascading water. Explore the pathways and enjoy the raw power of the falls. There's an entrance fee to access the best viewpoints.
spots.bestFor: Sightseers and those looking for a gentle walk with spectacular scenery.
spots.notSuitableFor: Those looking for a full gorge walking experience. This is more of a viewing point.
spots.parking: Designated car park near the entrance to Swallow Falls (charges apply).
spots.insiderTip: Visit after heavy rain for the most dramatic views of the falls. Be prepared for spray!
spots.access: Paid entry via the turnstile/kiosk at the dedicated Swallow Falls car park on the A5 between Betws-y-Coed and Capel Curig. Paths and viewing platforms only — there is no legal or safe way into the gorge itself here.

spots.name: Fairy Glen (Betws-y-Coed)
spots.description: A magical, sheltered gorge perfect for families with young children. The Fairy Glen features shallow water, easy scrambles, and moss-covered rocks that create a truly enchanting atmosphere. It's more of a paddling/wading experience than a true gorge walk.
spots.bestFor: Families with young children and those looking for a gentle introduction to gorge walking.
spots.notSuitableFor: Adrenaline junkies or those seeking a challenging adventure.
spots.parking: Small car park near the entrance (charges apply). Space is limited, especially on weekends.
spots.insiderTip: Combine your visit with a walk through the surrounding woodland for a longer day out.
spots.howToDoIt: This is a wade-and-paddle outing rather than a full gorge walk: shallow water, easy scrambling over moss-covered rock, and no jumps of consequence. Trainers or old walking shoes are fine; a wetsuit is optional rather than essential outside the coldest months.
spots.access: Fairy Glen sits on private land with its own small car park reached down a narrow lane — space for only a handful of cars, and access for larger vehicles is tight. Entry is a small per-person cash fee collected on an honesty basis by the landowners. If the car park is full, park at the larger Conwy Falls car park instead and walk in through Gwydir Forest.
spots.routeDescription: A short, sheltered path drops steeply down through mossy woodland to the river, where the gorge narrows into a shallow, enclosed ravine — more atmosphere than adventure, but genuinely pretty, and easy enough for young children under supervision.

spots.name: Aberglaslyn Gorge (Beddgelert)
spots.description: A scenic gorge walk through the narrow Aberglaslyn Pass. This route involves some scrambling over rocks and wading through the river. The scenery is spectacular, with views of the surrounding mountains. Be aware of water levels, especially after rain.
spots.bestFor: Those with some previous experience of scrambling and gorge walking.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those with limited mobility.
spots.parking: Parking available in Beddgelert village (charges apply).
spots.insiderTip: Enjoy a post-walk ice cream in Beddgelert - Gelateria Beddgelert is a great option.
spots.howToDoIt: This route is walked, not waded — expect a proper riverside path with some exposed, rocky sections rather than an in-river scramble. Sturdy footwear with grip matters more here than wetsuit boots; metal handholds are fixed at the trickiest point where the path rounds an outcrop above the water.
spots.access: The path follows the old fisherman's trackbed alongside the Welsh Highland Railway line between Beddgelert and Nantmor (National Trust land). Start from Beddgelert village or the National Trust car park at Nantmor at the southern end; the path crosses the railway at one point, so stay alert for trains.
spots.routeDescription: The Aberglaslyn Pass narrows to a dramatic, steep-sided ravine with the Glaslyn thundering below — the path threads along the true right bank with the railway line for company, opening out into gentler valley walking as you approach Beddgelert.

spots.name: Conwy Falls Gorge
spots.description: Located near Betws-y-Coed, Conwy Falls offers a short, steep gorge walk with stunning views of the falls. There's a small cafe on site. The walk to the bottom of the falls is challenging, involving some scrambling and steps.
spots.bestFor: Those looking for a short but rewarding gorge walk with impressive waterfall views.
spots.notSuitableFor: Those with mobility issues or very young children.
spots.parking: Parking available at the Conwy Falls Forest Park (charges apply).
spots.insiderTip: Check the water levels before you go, as the gorge can be impassable after heavy rain.
spots.access: Entry is via a turnstile at the Conwy Falls Forest Park car park and café, a small per-person fee. The park currently runs a one-way path system to manage the narrow sections, and the site also serves as an alternative walk-in access point for Fairy Glen via Gwydir Forest.
spots.routeDescription: A steep, well-built path with steps drops through mixed woodland to a viewing platform below the main falls — a genuinely powerful cascade rather than a wadeable gorge, so treat this as a waterfall walk with a café attached, not a wet scramble.

spots.name: Nant Gwynant Gorge (requires experience)
spots.description: A more challenging gorge walk in the Nant Gwynant valley. This route involves deeper water, more significant jumps, and technical scrambling. It's best suited to experienced gorge walkers or those with a guide.
spots.bestFor: Experienced gorge walkers seeking a more challenging adventure.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those without a high level of fitness.
spots.parking: Limited parking along the roadside in the Nant Gwynant valley. Park responsibly.
spots.insiderTip: Consider doing this route with a guide, especially if you're unfamiliar with the area.
spots.howToDoIt: Expect a longer day than Ogwen: deeper pools, bigger jumps, and sustained technical scrambling between them, with fewer easy bail-out points if you decide a section isn't for you. This is where operators like Plas y Brenin pitch trips at people who've already done a beginner gorge day and want to progress.
spots.access: Roadside parking only along the Nant Gwynant valley (A498) — limited and informal, so park tight to the verge and don't block passing places or field gates.

spots.name: Dolgarrog Pipeline Gorge (Expert Only)
spots.description: This is for experts only, this gorge is technical with strong currents. Don't even think about trying it without proper experience and equipment. It follows the course of the old pipeline.
spots.notSuitableFor: Anyone without significant gorge walking experience
spots.parking: Park discreetly in Dolgarrog village, be respectful of locals
spots.insiderTip: This gorge is not for the faint-hearted. Serious risk of injury or death if attempted by inexperienced walkers. Local knowledge is essential.
spots.access: Approached from Dolgarrog village — park considerately and be mindful of residents; this is a working village, not a visitor car park. This route should only ever be attempted with an experienced, properly equipped canyoning team; it is not a self-guided or beginner option under any circumstances.

spots.name: Ceunant Mawr (Llanberis Waterfall Canyon)
spots.description: Ceunant Mawr — Welsh for 'great ravine' — is the dramatic waterfall canyon directly above Llanberis village, fed by the Afon Arddu draining Cwm Brwynog below the Llanberis Path. Most operators run it as a canyoning descent (rope-led abseils down a series of stepped falls into deep plunge pools) rather than an upward gorge walk, because the headwalls are too sheer to scramble up cleanly. The setting is exceptional — slate-quarry walls on one side, the Snowdon massif overhead — and the approach from the village is short. This is the standard 'next step up' from a beginner Ogwen day, and one of the best half-day canyoning trips in the UK.
spots.bestFor: Anyone who's done a guided gorge day and wants the canyoning grade-up; strong scramblers comfortable with abseils on rope
spots.notSuitableFor: Complete beginners, anyone uncomfortable with abseil descents or cold-water immersion, weak swimmers
spots.bestSeason: May-September (water level dependent; needs settled weather for safe descent)
spots.parking: Llanberis village (multiple pay-and-display car parks). Approach on foot from the village — operators meet at their HQ and shuttle as needed.
spots.insiderTip: This is run as canyoning, not gorge walking — you'll be abseiling rather than scrambling up. Book with an operator that specifies Ceunant Mawr by name on their itinerary; generic 'Snowdonia gorge' day tickets usually mean the easier Ogwen route.
spots.howToDoIt: Almost all operators run Ceunant Mawr as a canyoning descent rather than a gorge walk: a short approach on foot from Llanberis, then a series of rope-led abseils down the stepped falls into deep plunge pools below. It suits confident swimmers who are comfortable being lowered on a rope and dropping into cold water — not a first gorge experience.
spots.access: Approach on foot from Llanberis village; operators typically meet clients at their village HQ and walk the short distance to the canyon rather than driving. Park in one of Llanberis's pay-and-display car parks.

spots.name: Ogwen Valley Gorge (Upper)
spots.description: More challenging than the lower section. Significant jumps, deeper water, and more technical scrambling make this suitable only for experienced gorge walkers or those with a guide. The scenery, as always in Ogwen, is spectacular.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, families, or those with a fear of heights.
spots.parking: Ogwen Cottage car park (charges apply). Even more limited space than the lower section.
spots.insiderTip: Consider doing both the upper and lower sections as a full-day adventure.
spots.howToDoIt: The upper Ogwen section raises the stakes over the lower gorge with deeper pools, bigger jumps and more sustained scrambling between them — most groups do it as a guided add-on after the lower section rather than as a standalone beginner trip.
spots.access: Same start point as the lower gorge — Ogwen Cottage / Ogwen Centre car park — but continue further upstream. Space in the car park is even tighter than for the lower section since both routes share the same access.

practicalInfo.weather: Snowdonia's weather is notoriously unpredictable. Conditions can change rapidly, from sunshine to heavy rain in a matter of minutes. Check the forecast before you go and be prepared for all eventualities. Water levels can rise quickly after rain, making gorge walking dangerous.
gearChecklist: Wetsuit - Essential for warmth, even in summer.
Wetsuit boots - Provide grip and protect your feet from sharp rocks.
Buoyancy aid - Crucial for safety in deeper water.
Helmet - Protects your head from bumps and scrapes.
Gloves - Improve grip and keep your hands warm.
Dry bag - To keep valuables safe and dry.
Appropriate footwear - Sturdy trainers or walking boots that you don't mind getting wet.
Warm layers - Even with a wetsuit, you'll appreciate an extra fleece or base layer.
Towel and change of clothes - For after your adventure.
Snacks and water - To keep your energy levels up.

gettingThere.publicTransport: Bangor and Llandudno Junction are the nearest train stations. From there, local bus services (e.g., the Sherpa bus) provide access to many of the popular gorge walking areas.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Parking can be challenging, especially during peak season. Arrive early, park responsibly, and be prepared to walk a short distance to the gorge.

practicalInfo.safety: Gorge walking can be dangerous. Always check the weather forecast and water levels before you go. Never attempt a gorge walk alone. Wear appropriate safety gear, including a wetsuit, buoyancy aid, and helmet. Be aware of the risks of cold water immersion. In case of emergency, call 999 and ask for Mountain Rescue.

faqs.question: Is gorge walking in Snowdonia safe?
faqs.answer: Gorge walking inherently carries risks. Check conditions, never go alone, wear proper gear. Incidents happen every year, so respect the environment.

faqs.question: What is the best time of year to go gorge walking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: May to September is generally the best time. Water levels are typically lower, and the weather is more stable. However, even in summer, the water can be cold, so a wetsuit is essential.

faqs.question: Do I need a guide for gorge walking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: For beginners or those attempting challenging routes, a guide is highly recommended. They have local knowledge, expertise, and safety equipment. Operators like Plas y Brenin are great options.

faqs.question: What should I wear for gorge walking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: A wetsuit, wetsuit boots, buoyancy aid, and helmet are essential. Gloves are also recommended. Wear sturdy trainers or walking boots that you don't mind getting wet. Bring warm layers for before and after your adventure.

faqs.question: Are there any age restrictions for gorge walking?
faqs.answer: Age restrictions vary depending on the specific gorge and the operator. Generally, children should be at least 8 years old and accompanied by a responsible adult. Some gorges are not suitable for young children.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to go gorge walking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: You can gorge walk for free in many locations, but you'll need your own gear. Guided experiences typically cost between £60 and £80 per person. Parking charges may also apply.

faqs.question: What happens if the weather turns bad while I'm gorge walking?
faqs.answer: If the weather deteriorates, exit the gorge as quickly and safely as possible. Seek shelter and wait for the conditions to improve. If you are with a guide, follow their instructions.

faqs.question: Are there any easier options for gorge walking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Fairy Glen near Betws-y-Coed is a popular choice for families with young children. It offers shallow water and easy scrambles. The lower section of the Ogwen Valley gorge is also a good option for beginners.

postActivitySpots.name: Pete's Eats
postActivitySpots.description: Legendary climber's cafe in Llanberis. Famous for its giant portions and hearty meals. The perfect place to refuel after a day of gorge walking.

postActivitySpots.name: Caffi Siabod
postActivitySpots.description: A popular cafe in Capel Curig, serving delicious food and drinks. A great spot to relax and enjoy the stunning views after your gorge walking adventure.

postActivitySpots.name: Cobdens Hotel
postActivitySpots.description: A traditional hotel with a cosy bar and restaurant. A great place to enjoy a post-gorge walking pint and a hearty meal.

postActivitySpots.name: Ty Hyll Ugly House
postActivitySpots.description: A quirky cafe near Betws-y-Coed, known for its unusual architecture and delicious cakes. A great place to stop for a treat after exploring the Fairy Glen or Conwy Falls.

postActivitySpots.name: The Heights Hotel
postActivitySpots.description: A good place to grab a drink or meal at the top of the Llanberis Pass. Offers great views of the surrounding mountains.

postActivitySpots.name: The Saracens Head Hotel
postActivitySpots.description: A historic hotel in Beddgelert village, great for a hearty meal and pint after a trip to Aberglaslyn Gorge.

accommodation.name: Plas Curig Hostel
accommodation.description: A budget-friendly hostel in Capel Curig, offering dorm rooms and private rooms. A great base for exploring the Ogwen Valley.

accommodation.name: Bryn Tyrch Inn
accommodation.description: Traditional inn in Capel Curig, ideal for exploring the Ogwen Valley and surrounding areas. Serves great food and has a friendly atmosphere.

accommodation.name: Gwern Gof Isaf Campsite
accommodation.description: A simple, no-frills campsite in the Ogwen Valley, popular with climbers and outdoor enthusiasts. A great option for budget-conscious travelers.

accommodation.name: Pen y Gwryd Hotel
accommodation.description: Historic climbing hotel at the foot of Snowdon and Tryfan. Perfect base for gorge walking adventures in Ogwen valley. Full of mountaineering history.

accommodation.name: Llyndir Guest House
accommodation.description: A comfortable bed and breakfast in Llanberis, close to Snowdon and other outdoor activities. Offers great views and a warm welcome.

accommodation.name: YHA Snowdon Pen-y-Pass
accommodation.description: Located at Pen-y-Pass, a great spot to start various climbs, and within easy driving distance of several gorge walking spots. Basic but comfortable rooms and great mountain views.

events.name: Snowdonia Trail Marathon
events.description: A challenging trail marathon through the stunning Snowdonia National Park. While not directly gorge walking, the course passes through some beautiful valleys and offers stunning scenery.

events.description: A grueling challenge to climb all 14 mountains over 3000 feet in Wales within 24 hours. It requires excellent fitness and navigation skills. Some sections could include elements of scrambling similar to gorge walking.

topTips: Water level beats every other variable here. A dry forecast on the day means nothing if the previous 48 hours dumped rain on the catchment above — Ogwen, Llugwy and Glaslyn all spike fast and drain slow. If you're going self-guided, check the Natural Resources Wales river levels page (stations at Betws-y-Coed/Cwmlanerch and Llanrwst cover the Conwy and Llugwy catchments) before you commit.

Ogwen Cottage car park (run by Eryri/Snowdonia National Park Authority, not the National Trust) is card/app only — no cash — and charges around £6 for the day or £3 for four hours. It's also the smallest car park serving the busiest gorge, so arrive early or go late afternoon if you want a space at all.

Fairy Glen at Betws-y-Coed sits on private land with its own small car park and an honesty-style entry system — cash only, a per-person fee on top of the parking charge. If the little car park is full, Conwy Falls has a much bigger one and you can walk in through Gwydir Forest instead.

Ceunant Mawr above Llanberis is the natural 'next step' after a beginner Ogwen day, but it's almost always run as canyoning (rope-led abseils down the falls) rather than an upward gorge walk — the headwalls are too sheer to scramble. Book with an operator that names Ceunant Mawr specifically; a generic 'Snowdonia gorge day' booking usually means the easier Ogwen route.

The Aberglaslyn Pass route follows the old fisherman's path alongside the Welsh Highland Railway line between Beddgelert and Nantmor — it's a proper path with metal handholds on the exposed sections, not a riverbed scramble like the others, so temper expectations if you're after a wet gorge day.

Dolgarrog Pipeline Gorge is listed here for completeness, not as a suggestion. It has a history of serious incidents and is not a self-guided option under any circumstances — go only with an experienced canyoning team who know the line.

Cold water catches people out even in August — Snowdonia's higher gorge pools sit around 8-12°C year-round. A wetsuit isn't optional kit for comfort, it's what stops a fun day turning into a cold-shock emergency.

Pack a post-gorge change of clothes and stash it in the car. Pete's Eats in Llanberis and Caffi Siabod in Capel Curig are the obvious refuel stops, but neither wants you dripping through the door in a wetsuit.

firstTimer: Start at the Ogwen Valley Gorge (Lower) with a guide — it's the classic beginner introduction, with wading, easy scrambles and small jumps, and it's where operators like Mountainxperience run their standard trips.
Book ahead. Guided gorge days fill up on summer weekends, and self-guided access to the harder sections (Ogwen Upper, Nant Gwynant) isn't recommended without prior gorge or scrambling experience.

Wear a wetsuit even if the forecast is warm — the water in Snowdonia's higher pools stays cold (8-12°C) right through summer, and cold-water shock is the biggest real risk for a first-timer, not the scrambling.

Bring cash for Fairy Glen and coins for pay-and-display machines at Beddgelert and Conwy Falls — several of the smaller sites in this guide are cash-only or card-only in ways that aren't obvious until you arrive.

If you're nervous about jumps, say so before you start. Every operator will let you climb down instead of jumping into a pool — there's no requirement to leap, and guides would rather you opt out than hesitate mid-jump.

Check age and ability guidance before booking a family trip. As a rough rule, children need to be around 8 and comfortable in water; the Fairy Glen and lower Aberglaslyn sections are the gentlest options if you're unsure.
Arrive at Ogwen Cottage early — the car park is small, serves the most popular gorge in the valley, and is cashless, so have a card or the RingGo-style app ready before you drive up.

Pack a warm layer and a hot drink for after. Even in a wetsuit you'll be cold once you're out of the water, and the nearest proper warm-up (Pete's Eats, Caffi Siabod, or Cobdens Hotel) is a short drive, not a five-minute walk.
regular: Once you've done a guided Ogwen day, Ceunant Mawr above Llanberis is the natural progression — but go in knowing it's a canyoning descent (abseils down the falls), not an upward gorge walk, and book an operator who names it specifically.

Skip the crowds by going early morning or late afternoon at Ogwen — the same insider tip applies at Fairy Glen and Aberglaslyn, both of which get busy with sightseers (not just gorge walkers) through the middle of the day in summer.

After a wet week, check river levels before heading to Ogwen, Llugwy, or Glaslyn-fed gorges — the Natural Resources Wales gauges at Betws-y-Coed and Llanrwst are the quickest read on whether the water's dropped enough to be sensible.

July and August are the only realistic window for Dolgarrog Pipeline Gorge, when water levels are at their lowest — and even then, it's an expert-only, guided-team-only route, not a solo add-on to a normal trip.
Nant Gwynant is the quieter alternative to Ogwen for anyone with the experience to go without a full beginner group — deeper water, bigger jumps, and a fraction of the foot traffic.

Combine both sections of the Ogwen gorge (Lower then Upper) for a full-day outing if you're already experienced — most first-timers only do the lower half, so the upper section stays noticeably quieter even in peak season.

Conwy Falls and Fairy Glen both sit close enough together to combine in one visit — park at the bigger Conwy Falls car park and walk through Gwydir Forest to Fairy Glen rather than fighting for the small dedicated space there.

If you're gorge walking out of Llanberis, Joe Brown's and V12 Outdoor on the high street are worth a stop even if you've already got kit — both do repairs and boot fitting, useful if a wetsuit boot blows out mid-trip.
